Full text

Introduction

Humans uniquely solve large-scale coordination problems through social institutions such as states (Henrich & Muthukrishna, 2021; Wylie et al., 2025). These institutions are composed of official rules and regulations that prescribe and proscribe human behavior, allowing strangers (i.e., non-kin) to coordinate their actions, which is theorized to enable widespread human cooperation (Henrich & Muthukrishna, 2021). Codified rules, especially in contrast with social norms, explicitly articulate proscribed behaviors and are particularly easy to preserve and pass down (i.e., in laws and codes of conduct) and reduce uncertainty and prediction errors in other people's behavior (Hadfield & Weingast, 2012; Wheeler et al., 2020).

Rules also facilitate third-party punishment. They pre-specify and pre-justify the possible punishments that become available once they are broken (Wylie & Gantman, 2024; Wylie et al., 2025). Rule enforcement is therefore theorized to be essential for large-scale cooperation through disincentivizing unwanted behavior and deterring future violations (e.g., Bicchieri, 2006; Henrich & Muthukrishna, 2021; Kahan, 1999; Ostrom, 2005; Wylie & Gantman, 2024; Wylie et al., 2025).

In addition, rules serve to communicate which behaviors are morally and socially acceptable (e.g., Cushman, 2015; Hampton, 1984; McAdams, 2015; Sarin, 2023; Sunstein, 1996). Accordingly, rules are commonly understood as proscriptions against behavior that undermines welfare or the provision of public goods (Ostrom, 1990). This cooperative view of rules is shared by everyday people, who tend to view rules as prosocial tools designed to promote cooperation and order (Flanagan & Hannikainen, 2022; Hannikainen et al., 2021; Wylie & Gantman, 2023). Consistent with this intuition, people take rules seriously and follow them even when incentivized not to (Gächter et al., 2025), and experience cognitive conflict when they break them (Pfister et al., 2016; Pfister et al., 2019).

But not all rules proscribe cooperative or immoral behaviors. Some rules arbitrarily regulate seemingly inconsequential behaviors that offer no obvious cooperative benefits to group welfare, such as taboos against eating harmless foods, specific dress codes, constraints on language and gestures, and even access to essential public services (Boyd & Richerson, 1992; Köster et al., 2022; Moynihan et al., 2015). Their existence highlights that rules may serve functions other than promoting the division of public goods and preventing social harm, which people find worth implementing and keeping.

A possible function of arbitrary rules is the promotion of obedience more generally. Recent work suggests that while "silly" rules may appear arbitrary and inconsequential, they may play a role in maintaining social order by facilitating the generalized learning of rule compliance. Using multi-agent reinforcement learning, researchers found that adding "silly rules" (i.e., punishing agents who consume taboo berries that are not poisonous) into a system that already contains important rules (i.e., punishing agents who consume poisonous berries) improves compliance with the important rules (Köster et al., 2022). In other words, one explanation for the proliferation of silly or otherwise arbitrary rules is that they help agents in a society develop general compliance to rules independent of their cooperative functions. This motivation may help explain why institutions demanding high levels of obedience and conformity, such as the military, also tend to have more arbitrary rules and rituals (Gelfand, 2018).

Crucially, the use of arbitrary rules has implications for understanding the psychological appeal of authoritarian governance. Authoritarian governance is conventionally distinguished from democratic governance by whether the power exercised is arbitrary or rooted in egalitarian principles (Fuller, 1969; Scheppele, 2018). One core characteristic of authoritarian governance is the proliferation of arbitrary constraints and rules (Glasius, 2018). Indeed, a willingness to weaponize rules for personal motives is conceptually aligned with rising support for antidemocratic practices (e.g., bending the rules to consolidate political power and thwart political outgroup members; Cheung, 2018; Scheppele, 2018; Stenner, 2005; Voelkel et al., 2024).

Similarly, previous studies have shown that people who prioritize conformity and who care about existing social hierarchy are more likely to enforce rules pretextually (Wylie & Gantman, 2023; Wylie et al., 2025). Specifically, they found that participants higher in right-wing authoritarianism were more willing to enforce a phantom rule-a frequently broken and rarely enforced rule (e.g., jaywalking)-against an actor who had also violated an unrelated social norm, essentially using the phantom rule to arbitrarily punish conduct that fell outside its purview. These findings raise the possibility that individuals with greater preference for obedience may find arbitrary rules more appealing as it provides a way to pretextually punish non-conformists. This preference may in part explain why they favor forms of governance that impose and enforce such rules and their persistence.

Taken together, many rules, including seemingly arbitrary rules that serve no overt cooperative function, may serve to lend rules the appearance of order and legitimacy, while merely facilitating conformity for its own sake or allowing actors to punish non-conformists pretextually.

If fostering general compliance is what arbitrary rules do, then people with a greater preference for obedience and conformity (over autonomy and diversity)-a preference commonly associated with authoritarian tendencies (Feldman, 2003)-should find them more appealing and be more willing to incur a personal cost to implement them, even when they serve no overt cooperative functions. Furthermore, if finding arbitrary rules appealing reflects a broader authoritarian orientation, then this preference should also be associated with greater support for anti-democratic practices. We therefore examine whether individuals' willingness to pay to implement arbitrary rules is associated with individuals' preferences for obedience and their support for antidemocratic practices.

Research Overview

Despite a widespread belief in the utility of rules and rule-following for cooperation, arbitrary rules proliferate and persist. In this paper, we sought to understand why, and we present evidence that people are willing to incur a cost to implement arbitrary rules (i.e., rules that impose arbitrary constraints but do not meaningfully increase payouts for the Receiver) in a modified Dictator Game. These rules were validated in a high-stakes interactive oTree experiment: cooperative rules increased Allocators' offers and Receivers' payout while arbitrary rules did not (Study 1) and were further validated in a supplemental study (N = 329, Mage = 38.30, SDage = 12.33, Female = 47.42%) that participants generally perceived these rules to have relatively low utility (M = 3.73, SD = 1.59 out of a possible score of 9). Crucially, we found that buying arbitrary rules was associated with greater individual preference for obedience (Studies 2a-3) and support for anti-democratic practices (Studies 2a and 3). Importantly, we found that preference for obedience was uniquely associated with purchasing arbitrary rules, but not cooperative rules (Study 3).

Finally, we showed that people purchased arbitrary rules at higher rates than a separate sample forecasted (Study 4) suggesting that people generally underestimate others' willingness to implement arbitrary rules that serve no cooperative functions.

Study 1

We first conducted a preregistered high-stakes interactive study (https://osf.io/dt5xa/files/qwfj6?view_only=ff50df46247043889bbdf5981f0fc2db) to validate the key construct of our paradigm, that is to validate that the arbitrary rules indeed only serve to impose arbitrary constraints and do not increase cooperative outcomes while cooperative rules do.

Secondly, we sought to test whether people will pay to implement arbitrary rules, even when the stakes are high.

Method Transparency and Openness.

For all studies, we report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study. All pre-registrations, data, and analysis code are available online (https://osf.io/dt5xa/overview?view_only=ff50df46247043889bbdf5981f0fc2db). In conducting this research, we complied with APA ethical standards in the treatment of our human samples. The experiment protocols were all approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB 2019-0388).

Participants

We recruited 1,363 participants from China on Credamo, a survey company based in China (Mage = 30.37, SDage = 9.32; Female = 52.31%). An a priori power analysis in G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) indicated that it requires 259 participants per role per condition to detect a small Condition × Time interaction (f = 0.10) in a 3 × 2 mixed ANOVA with 95% power. We oversampled by around 20% in our data collection to account for participants dropping out due to a failure to connect them with another player or their partner dropping out midgame. Inclusion criteria included living in China, being Chinese-speaking, and being at least 18 years of age.

Participants who did not complete all four rounds of the game were automatically excluded from analysis.

Procedure

After obtaining informed consent, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: an arbitrary rules condition (NAllocator-Designer pairs = 271), a cooperative rules condition (NAllocator-Designer pairs = 271), or a no-rule condition (NAllocator = 279). In all conditions, the Receivers were bots. Each player played four rounds with a ¥20 RMB endowment per round given to the Allocator at the beginning of the game and they were asked to decide how much to give to the Receivers. This endowment is comparable to similar studies conducted in China using the standard Dictator Game and Ultimatum Game (Jiao & Zhao, 2023; Zhu et al., 2013) and is roughly equal to $10 USD adjusting for purchasing power parity (World Bank, 2024), representing a meaningful economic stake for participants in the local context. Designers in the cooperative rules and arbitrary rules conditions were asked to observe the first two rounds of the game and decide after the second round whether or not they would pay ¥4 RMB each to implement up to three rules. In all conditions, participants were informed that 1 in every 10 participants would be randomly selected through a lottery system to receive payment, and that one of the four rounds would be randomly chosen to be paid out if they are selected prior to the beginning of the game. This Between-subjects Random Incentivized System (BRIS) has been shown to elicit comparable results as paying all participants for every round (Clot et al., 2018).

No-rule condition. All participants were assigned the role of the Allocator. Allocators were given ¥20 RMB each round and were told they could choose any amount to split with the Receivers. In each round, participants were asked to enter the amount they wished to give to the Receiver in a textbox (e.g., Alam & Rai, 2025; "If selected for lottery bonus, how much do you want to give to the Receiver in this round?").

Cooperative and arbitrary rules conditions. In both the cooperative and arbitrary rule conditions, participants were randomly assigned the role of the Allocator or the Designer.

Allocators were given ¥20 RMB each round and were told they could choose any amount to split with the Receivers. The Designers were given ¥20 RMB at the beginning of the game. All participants were additionally told that midway through the game, the Designer could choose whether or not to pay to implement up to three rules. After observing the Allocator's behavior in Rounds 1 and 2, Designers chose whether or not to pay to implement up to three rules (at ¥4 RMB each) that would take effect in Rounds 3 and 4. Each rule was shown to the Designers one by one in random order, and they indicated whether or not they would implement each of them one by one (0 = No,1 = Yes). The rules in the arbitrary conditions were: 1) Players cannot make fractional offers (e.g., 3.2 cents), 2) Players cannot make the same offer twice in a row, and 3) Offers must be made within 10 seconds. The rules in the cooperative conditions were: 1) "Players must offer at least ¥6 RMB." 2) "Allocators retaining more than ¥40 RMB at the end of four rounds will have their highest payout round excluded from the lottery" 3) "The Receiver gets a bonus of ¥4 RMB at the end" (See Table 1 for a complete list of rule choices per condition.) Measures Allocators' Offers. Allocators' offers were recorded across four rounds. We then calculated a pre-rule (Round 1 and Round 2) and post-rule average (Round 3 and Round 4) for each Allocator.

Receivers' Earnings.

Receivers' earnings were recorded across four rounds. We then calculated a pre-rule (Round 1 and Round 2) and post-rule average (Round 3 and Round 4) for each Receiver.

Total Number of Rules Purchased.

The total number of rules participants paid to implement was calculated (range = 0 -3).

Rule Purchase (Binary).

We preregistered a binary variable denoting whether each participant had implemented at least one rule (0 = no rule,1 = at least one rule).

Preference for obedience. We measured preference for obedience using Feldman and Stenner's 4-item Child Rearing Values (CRV) scale (Feldman & Stenner, 1997). Participants were asked to select the quality they believed to be more important for a child to have out of a pair of qualities (e.g., obedience vs. self-reliance) in each item. Participants received one point for every obedient trait they selected (i.e., respect for elders, obedience, to be well-behaved, and good manners). Each participant's total score was calculated (0 -4).

Demographic Variables.

Participants were asked to provide their age (rounded to the nearest whole number), gender (1 = Man,2 = Woman,3 = Prefer not to say), political ideology (1 = extremely liberal,7 = extremely conservative).

Data Analysis

All data analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2020). For mean offers and mean earnings, we fitted a mixed-effects ANOVA with Time (pre-rule vs post-rule) as a within-subject factor, and Condition (No rule, Cooperative rules and Arbitrary rules) as a between-subjects factor.

We conducted a two-proportion z-test to test the difference in the proportions of Designer implementing at least one rule in the cooperative and arbitrary rule condition.

Results

As preregistered, we conducted a mixed-effect ANOVA on Allocator offers with Condition (arbitrary, cooperative, no rule) coded as a between-subjects factor and Time (pre-rules: Rounds 1-2 vs. post-rules: Rounds 3-4) coded as a within-subjects factor. We found a significant Condition × Time interaction (F(2, 818) = 69.92, p < .001, η²p = .146). A post-hoc simple effect test revealed that mean offers increased most strongly in the cooperative condition (Δ = +3.77, t(818) = 15.34, p < .001). Mean offers also slightly but significantly increased in the no-rule condition (Δ = +0.74, t(818) = 3.04, p = .002). However in the arbitrary rules condition, there was no significant change in mean offers from pre-rules and post-rules (Δ = -0.14, t(818) = -0.59, p = PEOPLE WILL BUY ARBITRARY RULES .558; see Figure 1 and Table S1 & Table S3 in Supplementary Material for descriptive statistics and ANOVA table). A preregistered parallel mixed ANOVA on Receiver earnings yielded similar results (see Figure 1, as well as Table S2 and Table S4 in Supplemental Materials, for descriptive statistics and ANOVA table).

In addition, a two-proportion z-test revealed that Designers in the cooperative condition were significantly more likely to implement at least one rule than those in the arbitrary condition (z = 4.35, p < .001, h = 0.38), indicating that participants were generally sensitive to the utility of the rules. Importantly, despite the substantially high stakes (¥20 RMB per round, with each rule costing ¥4 RMB from the Designer's own budget), we found that 190 out of 271 Designers (70.11%, 95% CI [64.41%, 75.25%]) in the arbitrary rules condition paid to implement at least one rule. In the cooperative rules condition, 232 out of 271 Designers (85.61%, 95% CI [80.93%, 89.29%]) implemented at least one rule.

Discussion

In sum, in Study 1, we randomly assigned participants to play a typical Dictator Game or a modified version of the game where the Designers could pay to implement either cooperative rules or arbitrary rules. Allocators in the cooperative condition and no rule condition both increased their offers to the Receivers in the second half of the Dictator Game-though those who saw cooperative rules became substantially more generous than those who saw none. Critically, Allocators in the arbitrary rules condition did not increase their offers in the second half, making arbitrary rules effectively worse than no rules at all in our study. These results confirm that cooperative rules significantly increased Allocator's generosity in a high-stakes context while arbitrary rules had no effects on cooperative outcome. In sum, we validated the key construct in our paradigm that the arbitrary rules indeed only served to impose arbitrary constraints but not cooperative function. Lastly, our findings also demonstrated people's willingness to pay for arbitrary rules even when the stakes were high.

Study 2a

Next, we sought to test the link between arbitrary rules and preference for obedience (preregistered on https://osf.io/dt5xa/files/bntxd?view_only=ff50df46247043889bbdf5981f0fc2db). We hypothesized that preference for obedience will be associated with greater willingness to pay to implement arbitrary rules (i.e., rule that serve only to impose arbitrary constraints but do not serve to enhance cooperative outcome) against a selfish Allocator. Given that arbitrary constraints are commonly associated with support for anti-democratic practices, we additionally tested whether it is also associated with willingness to pay to implement arbitrary rules.

Method Participants

We recruited a total of 540 self-identified United States partisans from Prolific (50% selfidentified Democrats and 50% self-identified Republicans). For reasons unknown, Qualtrics successfully recorded responses from only 534 participants (Female = 50.37%) via Prolific (Mage = 39.66, SDage = 12.81). Inclusion criteria: American citizens currently living in the U.S., being English-speaking, and being at least 18 years of age. Using a Monte Carlo simulation, it was determined that we needed a minimum of 150 participants to detect the main effect of preference for obedience in a Poisson regression with 80% power. We oversampled by tripling our sample size because we planned to examine two-and three-way interactions.

Procedure

After informed consent, participants were told that they would be linked with two other players in the Sharing Game and randomly assigned to one of three roles: the Allocator, the Receiver, or the Designer. In reality, they were always assigned the Designer, and the other two were bots. The Designer received 10 cents at the beginning of the game, and midway through the game (after the second round), they had the opportunity to buy new rules for the game. They were told that they would play with the same players in their assigned roles for a total of four rounds.

They were also told that at the end of the game, we would tally the money for each round and randomly pay out one round in real money. In reality, we predetermined that we would pay out round 2, which was before any of our participants could spend their endowment, and therefore all participants received a 10-cent bonus. After reading the instructions, participants were asked to create a username and were then linked with two other players in an ostensible chatroom (to enhance believability). After the first two rounds of the game-in which participants witnessed the Allocator make selfish offers (kept 9 cents and 8 cents out of 10 cents, for Rounds 1 and 2, respectively), they were asked to indicate whether or not they would like to pay to implement three arbitrary rules, the same rules from Study 1.

Each rule was shown to all participants one by one in random order. They were asked to indicate one by one whether or not they would like to pay 2 cents to implement each of the rules (0 = No,1 = Yes). Then, participants were shown the final two rounds of the game, where the Allocator kept 7 cents and 6 cents out of 10 cents, respectively. The Sharing Game then ended, and participants were told that we would pay out Round 2, so they would each receive a 10-cent bonus (see Figure 2 and Table 1 for of three conditions: 1) No-rule condition, arbitrary rule condition, or cooperative rule condition.

In all conditions, the Receivers (blue) were bots and passive recipients of the Allocators (red) offers. In the no-rule condition, there were no Designers (green), and each Allocator freely split 10 RMB with the Receiver. In Studies 2a -3, all participants played as the Designer (green) and saw only the arbitrary condition where they were asked to first observe two rounds of the game.

They saw the Allocator (red) acted unfairly. The Allocator (red) gave the Receiver (blue) 1 cent (kept 9 cents) in the first round and gave Receiver 2 cents (kept 8 cents) in the second round. Then the Designers were asked if they wished to pay (2 cents each) to implement up to 3 rules. Each rule was presented one by one, and their orders were randomized. After they made their choices, they observed two more rounds before the game ended. In Study 3, participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions where they either saw only arbitrary rules or only cooperative rules. See Table 1 for a complete list of rule choices per condition.

Measures Comprehension Checks.

Given the complexity of the game, we had two comprehension checks question to ensure participants understood the game. We asked participants to indicate whether it was true that each rule cost 2-cents to implement (1 = True,2 = False) and whether they could correctly identify the correct statement from three statements (1 = "The Allocator kept more than they gave",2 = "The Allocator gave more than they kept" and3 = "The Allocator split the money equally"). As preregistered, we conducted separate analyses using the full sample and after excluding those who failed any one of our comprehension checks. If the results were different, we will report results of samples separately. If not, we will report the result from the full sample.

Total Number of Rules Purchased.

The total number of rules participants paid to implement was calculated (range = 0 -3).

Rule Purchase (Binary).

We preregistered a binary variable denoting whether each participant had implemented at least one rule (0 = no rule,1 = at least one rule).

Preference for obedience. We measured preference for obedience using Feldman and

Stenner's 4-item Child Rearing Values (CRV) scale (Feldman & Stenner, 1997). Participants were asked to select the quality they believed to be more important for a child to have out of a pair of qualities (e.g., obedience vs. self-reliance) in each item. Participants received one point for every obedient trait they selected (i.e., respect for elders, obedience, to be well-behaved, and good manners). Each participant's total score was calculated (0 -4).

Support for anti-democratic practices. In addition to the same measures for rule purchasing behavior and preferences for obedience, we additionally adapted the anti-democracy scale to measure participants' general support of anti-democratic practices (Voelkel et al., 2024).

Nine items measured participants' attitudes toward bending the rules (e.g., breaking the laws, gerrymandering, harassment) in order to maintain political dominance of the political party they support and to punish the political party they oppose.

Data Analysis

All data analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2020). For count outcome variables (e.g., the total number of rules purchased), we fitted Poisson regression models with a log link and robust (sandwich) variance estimation. Models included an offset equal to the log of the number of trials (i.e., 3), and we further exponentiated all estimates to compute the incidence rate ratio (IRR). Since the results of all of our studies that included the comprehension checks were consistent (Study 2a, 2b, 3) whether or not we excluded participants who failed the comprehension checks, we report results from the full sample.

Deviation from Preregistration.

Although we preregistered that we would use separate binary logistic regression (purchasing at least one rule) and a standard Poisson model (total number of rules), we adjusted our analytic approach to better match the structure of our experimental task.

Since participants had a fixed number of opportunities to purchase rules (i.e., 3) making the total number of rules purchased a count outcome with known exposure, we instead modeled rule purchases using a Poisson regression using robust (sandwich) standard errors with an offset based on the number of trials. This approach allowed us to avoid losing information and risk of Type 1 errors in dichotomizing variables (Altman & Royston, 2006) and to avoid treating the outcome as an unbounded count (i.e., standard Poisson regression).

Results

Of the 534 participants who played the Sharing Game (Mage = 39.66, SDage = 12.81, Female = 50.37%), 259 (48.50%, 95% CI [44.29%, 52.74%]) of them bought at least one of the arbitrary rules-significantly greater than the predicted rate 32.93% according to a one-sample exact binomial test (p < .001).

Preference for obedience. As hypothesized, we found that greater preference for obedience was associated with paying to implement more arbitrary rules (B = 0.32, SE = 0.03, p < .001, IRR = 1.37, 95% CI [1.29, 1.46]; see Figure 3 and Table S5 in Supplementary Material for regression table ).

Support for anti-democratic practices and political ideology.

We further explored whether purchasing more arbitrary rules is related to support for anti-democratic practices (e.g., bending the law to oppress self-perceived political opponents) (Voelkel et al., 2024). When support for anti-democratic practices was added to the model, we found that individuals who more strongly endorsed anti-democratic practices were also more likely to pay to implement arbitrary rules (B = 0.12, SE = 0.03, p < .001, IRR = 1.12, 95% CI [1.05, 1.20]), while the effect of preference for obedience remained significant (B = 0.30, SE = 0.03, p < .001, IRR = 1.34, 95% CI [1.26, 1.44]; see Figure S1 and Table S6 in Supplementary Material).

When we included political ideology and partisan identity, in the model predicting rule-buying the effects of preference for obedience (B = 0.29, SE = 0.04, p < .001, IRR = 1.33, 95% CI [1.24, 1.44]) and support for anti-democratic practices (B = 0.13, SE = 0.04, p < .001, IRR = 1.14, 95% CI [1.06, 1.23]) both remained significant, whereas political ideology (B = -0.03, SE = 0.04, p = .346, IRR = 0.97, 95% CI [0.90, 1.04]) and party identification (B = 0.16, SE = 0.14, p = .261, IRR = 1.17, 95% CI [0.89, 1.54]) were non-significant (see Table 2) as were all interactions (see also Table S7 and S8 in Supplementary Material). level of preference for obedience.

Panel (a-c) depicts the estimated association between preference for obedience and number of rules purchased in Studies 2a, 2b and 3, respectively. Lines represent model-estimated trends with shaded bands indicating 95% confidence intervals. Panel (d-f) depicts the density distribution of the number of rule(s) purchased (0 -3) at each level of preference for obedience score (0 -4) in Studies 2a, 2b and 3, respectively. Shaded regions represent the relative frequency of rule-purchase count at each preference for obedience level, with higher peak indicating greater relative frequency.

Discussion

In Study 2a, we conducted a study on Prolific to examine whether participants are willing to pay to implement arbitrary rules against a selfish Allocator. We hypothesized and found that willingness to buy more arbitrary rules was associated with both preferences for obedience and support for anti-democratic practices, after controlling for left-right ideology and partisanship.

More importantly, even though rules are often understood as a tool to enhance cooperation (Flanagan & Hannikainen, 2022), close to half the participants in the U.S. was willing to pay to implement at least one arbitrary rule in the game.

Study 2b

In Study 2b, we sought to replicate our findings from Study 2a in mainland China (https://osf.io/dt5xa/files/v4a7m?view_only=ff50df46247043889bbdf5981f0fc2db) via Credamo. Prior research has shown that cultural norms around authority, obedience, and the people's view of rules differ meaningfully across societies (Hofstede, 2001; Markus & Kitayama, 1991). In China, Confucian traditions and communist history emphasize it as a moral duty to conform to collective expectations and goals (Zhai, 2017), which may cultivate a broader tendency toward rule-following and deference to authority or a preference for greater norm conformity (or "tightness") (Gelfand et al., 2011). Yet, despite these cultural differences, we hypothesized that preferences for obedience would function similarly across the U.S. and China. That is, individuals who are more inclined toward obedience should be more likely to purchase arbitrary rules against an unfair Allocator-even in China, where rule-following is more culturally normative-because the motivation to enact rules for the extra-textual functions they permit would still be especially pronounced among those who value social order and obedience over autonomy (Feldman, 2003; Stenner, 2005). We hypothesized that the same underlying psychological mechanisms hold in a high-authority, collectivist society such that greater preference for obedience will be associated with paying for more arbitrary rules.

Method

Participants.

We recruited a total of 540 participants from China on Credamo, a survey company based

Measures.

We did not measure support for anti-democratic practices in Study 2b as they do not apply to the Chinese context. All other measures are translated from the same measures as Study 2a.

Data Analysis

The same statistical procedures from Study 2a were used.

Results.

First, we found that the rate of rule implementation in China was about two-thirds. Out of 540 people, 351, or 65% (95% CI [60.88%, 68.90%]), of the people paid to implement at least one arbitrary rule. Crucially, the rate of rule purchase is comparable to Study 1's (70.11%, 95% CI [64.41%, 75.25%]) which was also conducted in China, indicating that the endowment and payout system did not have a substantial effect on the rate of rule purchasing. We also replicated that higher preference for obedience was significantly associated with paying to implement more arbitrary rules in China (B = 0.22, SE = 0.04, p < .001; IRR = 1.24, 95% CI [1.14, 1.35]; see Figure 3 and Table S9 in Supplementary Material for regression table), suggesting that the relationship between preference for obedience and a willingness to pay for arbitrary rules against an unfair

Allocator generalizes across both cultural contexts.

Comparing the United States and China.

We conducted additional exploratory analyses to assess whether there was a statistically significant country difference in the rate of purchasing arbitrary rules and whether this difference could be explained by their preference for obedience. First, we found a main effect of country (0 = U.S.,1 = China) on the number of rules purchased, such that Chinese participants paid to implement more arbitrary rules than American participants (B = 0.41, SE = 0.07, p < .001; IRR = 1.50, 95% CI [1.32, 1.71]). Chinese participants also reported significantly higher preference for obedience than American participants according to a Welch t-test (t(862) = -2.48, p = .01, d = 0.15). Finally, a nonparametric mediation analysis with a generalized linear outcome (5,000 bootstrap) indicated that the association between country and total number of rules implemented was partially mediated by preference for obedience (indirect effect = 0.05, 95% CI [0.01, 0.10]), while the direct effect remained significant (direct effect = 0.42, 95% CI [0.29, 0.54]). This suggests that the country-level difference in arbitrary rule purchase can be partially explained by PEOPLE WILL BUY ARBITRARY RULES differences in preference for obedience embedded within these broader cultural contexts (see Figure 4). purchasing. Unstandardized path coefficients are shown, with 95% confidence intervals in brackets. Country was coded as0 = United States and1 = China. The direct effect of country on the number of rules purchased and the indirect effect via preference for obedience are reported below the diagram. Estimates are based on 5,000 nonparametric bootstrap samples.

Discussion

In Study 2b, we conducted a replication study on Credamo in China. Indeed, we replicated our main finding in Study 2a. Buying more arbitrary rules was also associated with preferences for obedience in China. Moreover, we found that a greater proportion of participants in China were willing to pay for these arbitrary rules and this difference can be partially explained by countrylevel differences in preference for obedience. In sum, we replicated our findings in Study 2a in a high-authority, collectivist society, offering a stringent test of the robustness and scope of our findings. Our exploratory finding shows that preference for obedience may not only explain within-country variability in the desire to implement arbitrary rules but may partially explain the country-level differences as well.

Study 3

Thus far, we have shown that preference for obedience (in the U.S. and China) and support for anti-democratic practices in the U.S. were associated with purchasing arbitrary rules in our Sharing game. It is, however, possible that preference for obedience is simply associated with greater willingness to implement any rules, cooperative and arbitrary alike. Therefore, in Study 3 (preregistered on https://osf.io/dt5xa/files/h4uxc?view_only=ff50df46247043889bbdf5981f0fc2db), we sought to specifically test whether this relationship is specific to arbitrary rules but not cooperative ones.

Method Participants

We recruited 540 self-identified partisans from Prolific (50% self-identified Democrats and 50% self-identified Republicans), following the same sample size rationale as Study 2a. In total, 538 completed our survey from Prolific (Mage = 40.73, SDage = 12.87, Female = 49.26%). Inclusion criteria included American citizens currently living in the U.S., English-speaking, and at least 18 years of age.

Procedure

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: an opportunity to buy either cooperative or arbitrary rules (see Figure 2 and Table 1 for rule options). In both conditions, participants saw the same non-conforming Allocator who kept 9 cents and 8 cents in the first two rounds respectively. The price of each rule was kept identical to Study 2a, and we used the same measures and data analysis from Study 2a.

Arbitrary Condition.

The procedure was identical to Study 2a also conducted in the U.S.

Cooperative Condition. The procedure was similar to Study 2a except that we replaced the three arbitrary rules with cooperative rules from Study 1. Furthermore, we modified Rule 2 in the cooperative condition relative to Study 1. Specifically, we replaced it with the standard Ultimatum Game rejection rule: "Give the Receiver the option to reject the offer; if they do so, both players receive nothing." We used the equal-split rule in Study 1 because the aim of it was to examine cooperative outcomes (i.e., Allocators' offers and Receivers' earning) and we had to avoid introducing a confound whereby the rule's effectiveness is depended on whether the Receiver actually utilizes the rejection option in repeated rounds-something we could not credibly simulate with the bot-Receivers. In Study 3, where our focus is on the Designers' rule purchase behavior, we therefore adopted the canonical Ultimatum Game rule, which carries much greater external validity on its cooperative function (e.g., Forsythe et al., 1994; Güth et al., 1982) and serves as a more stringent contrast with our arbitrary rules (see Table 1 for a list of the rules used in each study).

Results

First, we found a main effect of condition such that people paid for more cooperative rules than arbitrary rules (B = 0.49, SE = 0.09, p < .001, IRR = 1.64, 95% CI [1.37, 1.96]), in line with our findings from Study 1 that participants are generally sensitive to the utility of rules.

Specifically, of 269 participants in the cooperative rule condition, 213 (79.18%, 95% CI [73.94%, 83.61%]) paid to implement at least one cooperative rule. In the arbitrary rule condition, 134 out of 269 people (49.81%, 95% CI [43.88%, 55.75%]) paid to implement at least one rule.

We also found main effects for both preference for obedience (B = 0.09, SE = 0.03, p < .001, IRR = 1.10, 95% CI [1.04, 1.16]) and support for anti-democratic practices (B = 0.16, SE = 0.04, p < .001, IRR = 1.17, 95% CI [1.09, 1.26]). Most importantly, we found a significant preregistered interaction effect between preference for obedience and condition (B = -0.12, SE = 0.05, p = .033, IRR = 0.89, 95% CI [0.80, 0.99]; see Figure 3 and Table S10 in Supplementary Material for regression table ), such that the association between preference for obedience and rule purchasing depended on whether participants were in the arbitrary condition (simple slope for arbitrary condition: B = 0.17, SE = 0.05, p < .001, IRR = 1.18, 95% CI [1.08, 1.29]; simple slope for cooperative condition: B = 0.05, SE = 0.03, p = .09, IRR = 1.05, 95% CI [0.99, 1.11]). We found that preference for obedience was positively associated with buying arbitrary rules but not cooperative ones. The interaction effect of support for anti-democratic practices and condition was non-significant (B = -0.09, SE = 0.08, p = .291, IRR = 0.92, 95% CI [0.78, 1.08]; see Table S11 in Supplementary Material for regression table ).

Discussion

In Study 3, we sought to test whether willingness to pay for more arbitrary rules was uniquely associated with preference for obedience using a between-subjects design, where participants assigned as Designers saw either cooperative or arbitrary rules. We found that willingness to pay for more arbitrary rules was uniquely and more strongly associated with preference for obedience, showing that preference for obedience is tied specifically to rules that impose arbitrary constraints without improving cooperative outcomes, and that its association cannot be explained simply by a general appetite for rules. However, we did not observe the same interaction effect with anti-democratic practices, which suggests that support for anti-democratic practices reflected a general willingness to impose rules on a non-conforming Allocator, regardless of the rules' functions and content.

Study 4

The dominant perspective in research on third-party punishment and rule enforcement holds that rules are implemented to serve cooperative ends-such as deterring antisocial behavior and maintaining moral order (Fehr & Gächter, 2002; Tomasello, 2009 Tomasello, , 2016) ) and indeed lay people PEOPLE WILL BUY ARBITRARY RULES across cultures share the same intuition (Flanagan & Hannikainen, 2022). Given the prevailing perspective, a key question is whether people expect others to purchase arbitrary rules in our paradigm at all (see Figure 2). To assess this baseline expectation, we ran a separate preregistered forecasting study (https://osf.io/ya7ht?view_only=ff50df46247043889bbdf5981f0fc2db) on Prolific prior to conducting our pre-registered studies to test whether people generally underestimate others' willingness to implement these rules. We hypothesized that the expected rate would be lower than the actual rate of rule implementation, showing that people generally underestimate others' willingness to pay for arbitrary rules. Specifically, we preregistered that we would accept the result as aligning with our prediction if the participants' purchasing rate is higher than the high-end of the 95% confidence interval of the estimated rate.

Deviation from Preregistration.

In addition to our preregistered comparison between the baseline rate and actual rate in Study 2a, we conducted supplementary comparisons between the baseline rate and the actual rates from each of our preregistered studies with the same design (Studies 2a, 2b, 3).

Method Participants

We recruited 300 participants from Prolific (Mage = 45.64, SDage = 16.22, Female = 49.67%). Inclusion criteria included American citizens currently living in the U.S., Englishspeaking, and at least 18 years of age.

Procedures

We described the arbitrary rules condition of our Sharing Game (Study 2a) to participants in detail. Specifically, they were told that in this game, people were randomly assigned to three roles: Allocator, Receivers, and The Designer. Allocators were each given a 10 cents USD endowment at the beginning of each round and asked to decide how they wish to split the money with the Receivers for a total of four rounds. We explained that the Designers' job was to first observe the game and decide whether or not to implement the arbitrary rules (identical to Study 1). We further explained that in the first two rounds, the Designers in the game saw an Allocator who kept 9 cents and 8 cents, respectively. We then asked participants to guess how many people out of 100 they thought would pay to add at least one arbitrary rule to the game against an unfair Allocator.

Data Analysis

We first calculated the proportion of participants who implemented at least one rule in each sample, along with their corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Each study's observed proportion (p̂) was then statistically compared to the predicted proportion (i.e., p₀ = 0.329) and its associated 95% confidence interval. We then formally tested whether each observed proportion exceeded the forecasted baseline proportion (p₀ = 0.329) using one-sample exact binomial tests.

Results

The average prediction was 32.93% (95% CI [30.05%, 35.80%]) or around 33 out of 100 people. In addition to our preregistered comparison, we conducted supplementary comparisons between the proportions of people implementing at least one rule in each of our preregistered studies and the baseline predicted rate. According to a series of one-sample exact binomial tests, across all preregistered studies, the observed rates of rule implementation were significantly greater than the forecasted baseline (see Figure 5). studies. Blue points indicate the observed proportion of participants who purchased at least one rule in Studies 2a -3. Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals. The dashed horizontal line indicates the mean forecasted baseline proportion (32.93%, 95% CI [30.05, 35.80]), and the shaded band represents the 95% confidence interval. One-sample exact binomial tests show that the actual rate of purchasing at least one rule in all three studies exceeded the forecasted (***p < .001).

Discussion

In Study 4, we formally tested whether people underestimate others' willingness to implement arbitrary rules in our version of the Sharing game. Our results showed that the baseline forecasted rate was significantly lower than the actual implementation rates across all our preregistered studies where participants saw a non-conforming Allocator. The result highlights that people generally underestimate others' willingness to purchase arbitrary rules that serve no overt cooperative functions. Yet, across our pre-registered studies, half to two-thirds (48.50% -65%) of the participants were willing to pay for at least one of these arbitrary rules even when the stakes were high.

Internal Meta Analysis

Finally, we conducted an internal meta-analysis to estimate the pooled effect of the positive association between preference for obedience and arbitrary rule purchasing among the four studies sharing the same design: participants were always assigned the Designer role, observed a nonconforming Allocator, and decided whether or not to purchase the same three arbitrary rules. This method allowed us to compute a single estimate of the association with greater precision as well as a prediction interval showing the range of possible effects that one would expect in a new sample. We have included all experiments we ran with this paradigm including our pilot work to mitigate selection bias. Additionally, this method allows us to not rely only on individual effects and p-values of individual studies (Goh et al., 2016). It is important to note that with a small number of studies, we recognize that the Egger's test and heterogeneity estimate may be unreliable and should be interpreted with caution.

Data Analysis

To estimate the overall association between preference for obedience and arbitrary rule implementation across all four studies with the same paradigm (Study 2a, Study 2b, Study 3, and a supplemental pilot studyfoot_0 ), we conducted a mini meta-analysis using the metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010) and meta (Balduzzi et al., 2019) packages in R. We extracted the log-transformed incidence rate ratios and their corresponding standard errors from four independent studies. A random-effects model was fitted using restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML) to account for potential between-study heterogeneity. Heterogeneity was evaluated using the Q statistic, tau², and I² metrics. Egger's regression test was used to assess the possibility of publication bias.

Results

A random-effects meta-analysis found a significant positive association between preference for obedience and arbitrary rule implementation. The effect corresponds to a 28% increase in the rate of rule implementation for each unit increase in preference for obedience (IRR = 1.28, 95% CI [1.20, 1.37]; see Figure 6). The heterogeneity test showed substantial heterogeneity across studies (I² = 63.2%, τ² = 0.003, p = .04). The prediction interval [1.04, 1.58] using a t distribution with k -1 degrees of freedom indicated that preference for obedience is expected to have a positive association with rule purchasing across the study populations though the magnitude of the effect varied across contexts. Egger's regression test and visual inspection of the funnel plot were used to examine potential publication bias. Egger's test indicated no evidence of funnel plot asymmetry (t(2) = -0.90, p = .461).

Discussion

The positive association between preference for obedience and arbitrary rule purchasing held across studies. The magnitude of the effect varied considerably (I² = 63.2%) but the prediction interval [1.04, 1.58] remained above 1. Thus, our test showed that even after adjusting for the variation, a positive association between preference for obedience and arbitrary rule purchasing would be expected in a new sample. for obedience and the number of rules purchased. Grey squares indicate IRR estimates, and horizontal lines represent 95% confidence intervals. Square size reflects inverse-variance weighting. The grey diamond represents the pooled estimate from a random-effects model, with its width indicating the 95% confidence interval. Heterogeneity statistics (I², τ², and p value) are shown below the plot. Estimates are based on Poisson regression models across three preregistered studies and one supplemental study.

General Discussion

People commonly assume that rules exist to promote cooperation. This likely explains why people are inclined to make and follow rules (Gächter et al., 2025). Across four preregistered studies in which participants could buy rules (plus a preregistered forecasting study and an internal meta-analysis), including participants in both the United States and mainland China, we find that people are willing to pay to enact rules in a Dictator Game that neither make the game fairer nor promote cooperation. People generally underestimate others' willingness to enact such rules. We also hypothesized and found that people with a greater preference for obedience, in both the United States and China, are especially willing to pay for these arbitrary rules. Moreover, we found that preference for obedience significantly mediated the relationship between country and rule implementation, suggesting that this preference explains may not only within-country variation in arbitrary rule implementation but also some of the cross-cultural variance. Finally, we also found evidence of discriminant validity such that people with a higher preference for obedience were more likely to buy arbitrary, but not cooperative, rules. In sum, despite the widespread assumption that rules mostly support cooperation and promote fairness (e.g., Fehr & Gächter, 2002; Tomasello, 2016), our results show that substantial amount of people in both U.S. and China will buy rules that do not promote cooperation or enhance fairness. Importantly, we found that a psychological tendency toward obedience-often theorized to be related to authoritarianism (e.g., Feldman & Stenner, 1997; Stenner, 2005)-predicts the purchasing of these rules.

Implications

Our findings build on prior work on people's general desire for rules and willingness to follow them (Gächter et al., 2025; Pfister et al., 2016), as well as the relatively hidden functions of "silly rules" (Köster et al., 2022), proxy crimes (Bystranowski, 2017), and selectively punished "phantom rules" (Wylie & Gantman, 2023), as well as challenge the widespread understanding of rules as a tool that serves primarily to promote cooperation and social order (e.g., Fehr & Gächter, 2002; Tomasello, 2016). Our findings also hint at where arbitrary rules may be most useful. When a disliked conduct cannot be sanctioned directly because it may be difficult to codify, hard to prove, or formally protected (e.g., religious beliefs), a rule governing adjacent behaviors may provide a formally lawful route to regulate, inconvenience or punish the actor. It is important to note that rules that are enforced to selectively target non-conforming individuals rather than behaviors violate the basic tenets of a liberal legal order, such as the rule of law, which stipulates that rules must be publicly disclosed and applied equally to all without bias and favoritism (Fuller, 1969). When rules carry hidden functions and are used to constrain and punish targeted nonconforming individuals for behaviors that are outside of the purview of the said rules, they can easily become a tool of control and domination rather than a tool of cooperation (Foucault, 1977; Wylie & Gantman, 2024). In this way, our findings speak to understanding the appeal of authoritarianism as evidenced in rising autocracy and democratic backsliding around the globe, especially within liberal institutions wherein constitutional or legal means are used to quash political dissenters and consolidate centralized political power (Pascale, 2019; Scheppele, 2018).

Here we capture this desire to implement official rules of otherwise little utility against a nonconformist in a minimal context and show that this behavior is related to preference for obedience (i.e., authoritarianism) and support for anti-democratic practices.

Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations are worth noting. First, our game gives participants the option to buy rules for themselves, which few have the opportunity to do at the state or national level. Second, our findings on the association between a preference for obedience and the implementation of arbitrary rules are correlational. Future research should experimentally induce a desire for conformity and control, such as through inducing a sense of anomie-which has previously been found to be associated with support for authoritarianism and strong leadership (e.g., Neerdaels et al., 2026; Sprong et al., 2019)-to test a causal relationship between need for social control and arbitrary rule enactment. Third, the present studies focused on a relatively small set of arbitrary and cooperative rules within a simplistic environment using the Dictator Game paradigm. This approach enabled us to maximize experimental control across studies and cultural contexts.

However, the simplicity of the paradigm inherently limits the range of behaviors over which PEOPLE WILL BUY ARBITRARY RULES meaningful constraints can be realistically imposed through an online experiment. Future research should examine a broader range of cooperative and arbitrary rules in other institutional environments and vignettes type studies to determine the generalizability of the present findings across contexts. Finally, here in this study, we focused on the association between preference for obedience and willingness to implement arbitrary rules against a non-conforming (i.e., unfair)

Allocator. Future research should test whether this result replicates in the face of other normative violations.

In sum, people in both the U.S. and China will buy arbitrary rules in an economic game.

Even though people generally believe that rules are meant to promote cooperation and underestimate others' willingness to implement arbitrary rules, many people across the U.S. and China will pay for rules that do not serve these functions. Crucially, people who prefer obedience and who endorse anti-democratic practices are more willing to enact these rules. For preference for obedience, this willingness was specific to arbitrary rules and did not extend to rules with more explicitly cooperative functions, highlighting that their attraction to these rules cannot simply be explained by a general appetite for rules.
